 Assessing Cost-Effectiveness of E-Dengue Early Warning System in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta

 Assessing Cost-Effectiveness of E-Dengue Early Warning System in Vietnam's Mekong Delta
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 Dengue fever continues to represent a substantial public health burden across tropical and subtropical regions, with the disease dynamics influenced significantly by urbanization, global mobility, and shifting climate patterns. In Vietnam, where the virus is endemic, the incidence of dengue displays considerable year-to-year variation, as illustrated by the Ministry of Health reporting figures ranging from over 69,000 to more than 345,000 cases annually between 2021 and 2025. Given that many infections result in mild or asymptomatic symptoms and are consequently never documented in formal surveillance systems, the actual number of annual cases is estimated to be significantly higher, reaching potentially millions. This heavy burden, measured in terms of mortality and disability-adjusted life years, has necessitated a shift toward more proactive and targeted prevention strategies, particularly in regions like the Mekong Delta, which frequently records the highest incidence rates nationwide.
 To address this challenge, researchers have developed the E-Dengue platform, an early warning system designed to predict potential epidemics up to three months in advance by utilizing a machine learning model integrated with historical epidemiological and environmental data. Developed under the “Useful, Usable, and Used” framework, the system is intended to translate sophisticated predictive outputs into actionable public health decisions at the Regional Health Center level. By focusing on predictive accuracy and seamless integration into routine surveillance workflows, the E-Dengue tool aims to bridge the long-standing gap between the availability of predictive modeling technology and its actual adoption in frontline dengue control practices, such as proactive source reduction and targeted community education campaigns.
 The current study protocol outlines a rigorous health economic evaluation conducted alongside a parallel-group, two-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial, which is currently registered under the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry. This trial, which spans two dengue seasons in 2026 and 2027, covers 118 Regional Health Centers across the Mekong Delta Region after excluding areas prone to contamination from other ongoing vaccine or mosquito-based intervention studies. By randomly allocating these centers to either the intervention or nonintervention arm, the investigators are creating a controlled environment to assess both the efficacy of the proactive E-Dengue alerts and the relative economic value of the system compared to existing routine prevention methods.
 The evaluation adheres to the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standard 2022, ensuring that the methodologies used are transparent, reproducible, and aligned with international best practices for health economic assessment. A key design feature is the adoption of a societal perspective, which is the most comprehensive approach for identifying all relevant costs associated with both the implementation of the E-Dengue system and the routine dengue control practices mandated by the Vietnamese government. This approach ensures that the analysis accounts for direct costs, such as the resources needed for software operation and intervention deployment, as well as the indirect burden of the disease on patients and their informal caregivers.
 Cost data collection is multi-faceted and relies on diverse financial sources, including project financial reports, health partner records, and structured surveys. For the operational costs of the E-Dengue tool, researchers are recording startup investments—including human resources, infrastructure, and equipment—which will be annualized using a 3% discount rate to accurately reflect their useful lifespan. In the intervention arm, costs for proactive measures such as source reduction and community loudspeakers are being meticulously tracked. Simultaneously, the costs of routine dengue prevention activities, including insecticide spraying and education campaigns performed in both arms, are being sourced from provincial Centers for Disease Control to provide an accurate baseline of existing investment.
 A critical component of the economic evaluation is the cost-of-illness substudy, which provides the evidence base for valuing the burden per dengue episode. Conducted at two hospitals in Dong Thap province, this cross-sectional survey targets a sample of 135 inpatients and 135 outpatients, along with their informal caregivers. The protocol defines informal caregivers through specific time-based criteria to distinguish them from casual visitors, ensuring that the valuation of productivity losses and nonmedical expenditures is both precise and relevant to the actual experience of patients within the local healthcare setting. These patient-level costs, combined with direct medical charges from hospital billing, allow for an estimation of the economic burden that remains even in the absence of the early warning system.
 The analysis of cost-effectiveness relies on seemingly unrelated regression models to estimate incremental costs and incremental health outcomes, such as disability-adjusted life years and dengue cases averted. This choice of statistical model is essential for managing the inherent correlation between cost and outcome variables at the cluster level within a randomized trial, while simultaneously adjusting for regional covariates like population density and historical outbreak frequency. By isolating the intervention effects in this manner, the investigators aim to provide a robust assessment of whether the E-Dengue system offers a clear incremental benefit that justifies the additional investment required for its implementation.
 Decisions regarding cost-effectiveness are centered on the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, which is compared against a pre-specified willingness-to-pay threshold. For the base case analysis, the team has chosen a threshold of 0.5 times the gross domestic product per capita, a standard supported by recent empirical data for low- and middle-income countries that suggests many conventional thresholds are insufficiently rigorous. The protocol further mandates a wide array of sensitivity analyses—including one-way and probabilistic Monte Carlo simulations—to explore how potential uncertainties in parameters like the expansion factor for unreported cases or variations in tool operating costs might influence the final determination of value for money.
 Limitations inherent in the study design, such as the focus on a single province for specific cost estimations or the challenges of separating dengue-specific infectious disease costs from overall surveillance budgets, are being addressed through these extensive sensitivity tests. By varying these parameters by one standard deviation or specific percentage intervals, the researchers are ensuring that the study’s conclusions remain reliable across a wide range of plausible scenarios. This cautious approach to modeling serves to enhance the credibility of the findings for policymakers who must make difficult resource allocation decisions in a resource-limited public health environment.
 The study’s potential impact is profound. If the trial demonstrates that the E-Dengue system is cost-effective, it will provide the evidence necessary to advocate for its large-scale integration into national routine surveillance and prevention programs in Vietnam. This would mark a significant advancement in shifting dengue control from a reactive to a proactive strategy. Furthermore, the detailed methodology developed in this protocol offers a valuable blueprint for evaluating other early warning systems and novel digital health technologies, contributing essential evidence to the global literature on the economics of infectious disease prevention and the practical application of real-time epidemic modeling.
 The operational protocol defines a strict timeline translating early warning predictions into field actions across designated health centers. Monthly forecasts generated three months in advance, such as using data through July to predict October epidemics by mid-August, trigger targeted interventions scheduled during the intervening month of September. Within alerted Regional Health Centers, resource constraints dictate that physical source reduction, carried out by community teams without chemical insecticides, focuses exclusively on communes accounting for at least fifty percent of historical caseloads. In contrast, educational communication campaigns are broadcast across all communes within the alerted district via municipal loudspeakers. To monitor vector density changes alongside these activities, provincial Centers for Disease Control staff conduct standardized larvae surveys one day prior to source reduction to establish a baseline, one day after to measure immediate impact, and three weeks post-intervention to assess temporal sustainability, matching parallel four-week larval surveys conducted in control districts.
 To accurately capture disease impact beyond formal hospital records, the evaluation framework applies empirical adjustments for routine surveillance underreporting. Between 2018 and 2024, ninety-three percent of dengue notifications in the Mekong Delta represented hospitalized patients, reflecting substantial undercounting of mild infections. Assuming that diagnostic testing limits and symptom overlap with other febrile illnesses result in misdiagnosis, researchers apply a 1.2 expansion factor to hospital admissions, projecting community-wide incidence based on established shares of 64.1 percent informal care, 23.3 percent outpatient care, and 12.6 percent inpatient admissions. When calculating primary health outcomes, disability-adjusted life years incorporate both premature mortality discounted at three percent annually and acute and persistent morbidity. Disability weights of 0.0307 for outpatient or informal cases and 0.0351 for inpatient admissions explicitly incorporate post-acute sequelae, reflecting observations that one-third of dengue patients endure lingering symptoms lasting an average of over eleven months.
 The economic methodology also incorporates structured rules to value productivity loss and handle potential trial ambiguities. Researchers estimate lost productivity using the human capital approach for salaried labor and the prevailing minimum wage under an opportunity cost approach for unpaid domestic work, while assigning a literature-derived cost of 17.32 US dollars per informal care episode. If trial results reveal that the early warning platform fails to achieve cost-effectiveness due to elevated implementation expenses or insufficient preventive efficacy, the investigators plan to model the system under varying hypothetical efficacy levels to determine the performance necessary for viability. Should substantial parameter uncertainty yield inconclusive findings, planned secondary subgroup analyses will identify key drivers of variance and determine whether the intervention proves economically favorable in specific high-burden operational contexts.
 Subject of Research: Economic evaluation of a proactive dengue early warning system in Vietnam.
 Article Title: Economic Evaluation of an E-Dengue Early Warning System for Proactive Dengue Prevention in the Mekong Delta Region, Vietnam: A Protocol
